From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Fiction in a setting defined in part by climate crisis

Not to be confused with [Climate change denial](/wiki/Climate_change_denial "Climate change denial").

<figcaption>A climate fiction depiction of agriculture in India in 2500, with workers wearing protective suits to protect from extreme temperatures and <a href="/wiki/Unmanned_ground_vehicle#Agriculture" title="Unmanned ground vehicle">drone tractors</a>.</figcaption>

| -   [v](/wiki/Template:Speculative_fiction_sidebar "Template:Speculative fiction sidebar")                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

**Climate fiction** (sometimes shortened to **cli-fi**) is [literature](/wiki/Literature "Literature") that deals with [climate change](/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}1[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:2-1)^ Generally [speculative](/wiki/Speculative_fiction "Speculative fiction") in nature but inspired by [climate science](/wiki/Scientific_consensus_on_climate_change "Scientific consensus on climate change"), works of climate fiction may take place in [the world as we know it](/wiki/Realism_(arts) "Realism (arts)"), in the [near future](/wiki/Near_future_in_fiction "Near future in fiction"), or in [fictional worlds](/wiki/Fictional_universe "Fictional universe") experiencing climate change. The genre frequently includes [science fiction](/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") and [dystopian or utopian themes](/wiki/Utopian_and_dystopian_fiction "Utopian and dystopian fiction"), imagining potential futures based on research about the [impacts of climate change](/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change_on_humans "Effects of climate change on humans"){.mw-redirect} and speculations about how humans may respond to these and the problem of climate change. Climate fiction typically involves [anthropogenic](/wiki/Human_impact_on_the_environment "Human impact on the environment") climate change and other environmental issues as opposed to weather and disaster more generally. Technologies such as [climate engineering](/wiki/Climate_engineering "Climate engineering"){.mw-redirect} or [climate adaptation practices](/wiki/Climate_change_adaptation "Climate change adaptation") often feature prominently in works exploring their impacts on society.

The publication of [Kim Stanley Robinson](/wiki/Kim_Stanley_Robinson "Kim Stanley Robinson")\'s *[The Ministry for the Future](/wiki/The_Ministry_for_the_Future "The Ministry for the Future")* in 2020 helped cement the genre\'s emergence; the work generated presidential and United Nations mentions and an invitation for Robinson to meet planners at the Pentagon.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}2[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Rothman-2)^ University courses on literature and environmental issues may include climate change fiction in their [syllabi](/wiki/Syllabus "Syllabus").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}3[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-3)^ This body of literature has been discussed by a variety of publications, including *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")*, and *[Dissent](/wiki/Dissent_(American_magazine) "Dissent (American magazine)")* magazine, among other international media outlets.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}4[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-4)^ Lists of climate fiction have been compiled by organizations including [*Grist*](/wiki/Grist_(magazine) "Grist (magazine)"), [*Outside* Magazine](/wiki/Outside_(magazine) "Outside (magazine)"), and the New York Public Library.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}5[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-5)^ Academics and critics study the potential impact of fiction on the broader field of [climate change communication](/wiki/Climate_communication "Climate communication").

## Use of the phrase {#Use_of_the_phrase}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Use of the phrase")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

The term \"cli-fi\" is generally credited to freelance news reporter and climate activist Dan Bloom, who coined it in either 2007 or 2008.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}1[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:2-1)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}6[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-AsTheWeatherShifts-6)^ References to \"climate fiction\" appear to have begun in the 2010s, although the term has also been retroactively applied to a number of works.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}7[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:3-7)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}8[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:1-8)^ Pioneering 20th century authors of climate fiction include [J. G. Ballard](/wiki/J._G._Ballard "J. G. Ballard") and [Octavia E. Butler](/wiki/Octavia_E._Butler "Octavia E. Butler"), while dystopian fiction from [Margaret Atwood](/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") is often cited as an immediate precursor to the genre\'s emergence. Since 2010, prominent cli-fi authors include [Kim Stanley Robinson](/wiki/Kim_Stanley_Robinson "Kim Stanley Robinson"), [Richard Powers](/wiki/Richard_Powers "Richard Powers"), [Paolo Bacigalupi](/wiki/Paolo_Bacigalupi "Paolo Bacigalupi"), and [Barbara Kingsolver](/wiki/Barbara_Kingsolver "Barbara Kingsolver").

Bloom had used the term to describe his novella *Polar City Red*, a post-apocalyptic story about [climate refugees](/wiki/Climate_refugees "Climate refugees"){.mw-redirect} in Alaska set in 2075, which was not commercially successful.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}1[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:2-1)^ It later came into mainstream media use in April 2013, when *[Christian Science Monitor](/wiki/Christian_Science_Monitor "Christian Science Monitor"){.mw-redirect}* and [NPR](/wiki/NPR "NPR") ran stories about a new literary movement of novels and films that dealt with human-induced [climate change](/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}1[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:2-1)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}7[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:3-7)^ Bloom had been critical of the lack of mention of his role in coining the term in these features.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}1[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:2-1)^ Scott Thill wrote in *[HuffPost](/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")* in 2014 that he had popularised the term in 2009, inspired by the mixture of science and fiction in [Franny Armstrong](/wiki/Franny_Armstrong "Franny Armstrong")\'s film *[The Age of Stupid](/wiki/The_Age_of_Stupid "The Age of Stupid")*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}9[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-9)^

## History {#History}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

[Jules Verne](/wiki/Jules_Verne "Jules Verne")\'s 1889 novel *[The Purchase of the North Pole](/wiki/The_Purchase_of_the_North_Pole "The Purchase of the North Pole")* imagines climate change due to [tilting of Earth\'s axis](/wiki/Earth#Axial_tilt_and_seasons "Earth").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}10[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-10)^ In his posthumous *[Paris in the Twentieth Century](/wiki/Paris_in_the_Twentieth_Century "Paris in the Twentieth Century")*, written in 1863 and set during the 1960s, the eponymous city experiences a sudden drop in temperature, which lasts for three years.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}11[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-11)^

[Laurence Manning](/wiki/Laurence_Manning "Laurence Manning")\'s 1933 serialized novel *[The Man Who Awoke](/wiki/The_Man_Who_Awoke "The Man Who Awoke")* has been described as an exemplary work of ecological science fiction from the golden age.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}12[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-12)^ It tells the story a man who awakes from [suspended animation](/wiki/Suspended_animation "Suspended animation") in various future eras and learns about the destruction to the Earth\'s climate, caused by overuse of fossil fuels, [global warming](/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming"){.mw-redirect}, and [deforestation](/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation"). People of the future refer to 20th century humans as \"the wasters\". They have abandoned over-industrialization and [consumerism](/wiki/Consumerism "Consumerism") to live in small self-sufficient villages based around genetically engineered trees that provide all their necessities. [Isaac Asimov](/wiki/Isaac_Asimov "Isaac Asimov") credited *The Man Who Awoke* for bringing the \"[energy crisis](/wiki/1970s_energy_crisis "1970s energy crisis")\" to his attention 40 years before it became common knowledge in the 1970s.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}13[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-13)^

<figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Amitav_Ghosh_-_River_Of_Smoke_2011_a_crop.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Amitav_Ghosh_-_River_Of_Smoke_2011_a_crop.jpg/250px-Amitav_Ghosh_-_River_Of_Smoke_2011_a_crop.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="2675" data-file-width="1783" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Amitav_Ghosh_-_River_Of_Smoke_2011_a_crop.jpg/330px-Amitav_Ghosh_-_River_Of_Smoke_2011_a_crop.jpg 2x" width="150" height="225" /></a>
<figcaption>In 2016, Indian writer <a href="/wiki/Amitav_Ghosh" title="Amitav Ghosh">Amitav Ghosh</a> described a lack of coverage of climate change in contemporary fiction as "<a href="/wiki/The_Great_Derangement:_Climate_Change_and_the_Unthinkable" title="The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable">the great derangement</a>".</figcaption>
</figure>

Several well-known [dystopian](/wiki/Dystopia "Dystopia") works by British author [J. G. Ballard](/wiki/J._G._Ballard "J. G. Ballard") deal with climate-related natural disasters. In *[The Wind from Nowhere](/wiki/The_Wind_from_Nowhere "The Wind from Nowhere")* (1961), civilization is devastated by persistent hurricane-force winds, and *[The Drowned World](/wiki/The_Drowned_World "The Drowned World")* (1962) describes a future of melted ice-caps and [rising sea-levels](/wiki/Rising_sea_levels "Rising sea levels"){.mw-redirect} caused by [solar radiation](/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}14[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-14)^ In *[The Burning World](/wiki/The_Burning_World_(novel) "The Burning World (novel)")* (1964, later retitled *The Drought*) his climate catastrophe is human-made, a [drought](/wiki/Drought "Drought") due to disruption of the precipitation cycle by [industrial pollution](/wiki/Pollution "Pollution").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}15[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-15)^

[Frank Herbert](/wiki/Frank_Herbert "Frank Herbert")\'s 1965 science fiction novel [*Dune*](/wiki/Dune_(novel) "Dune (novel)"), set on a [fictional desert planet](/wiki/Arrakis "Arrakis"), has been proposed as a pioneer of climate fiction for its themes of ecology and environmentalism.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}8[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:1-8)^

[Octavia E. Butler](/wiki/Octavia_E._Butler "Octavia E. Butler")\'s *[Parable of the Sower](/wiki/Parable_of_the_Sower_(novel) "Parable of the Sower (novel)") (*1993) imagines a near-future for the United States where climate change, wealth inequality, and corporate greed cause apocalyptic chaos. Here, and in sequel [*Parable of the Talents*](/wiki/Parable_of_the_Talents_(novel) "Parable of the Talents (novel)") (1998), Butler dissects how instability and political demagoguery exacerbate society\'s underlying cruelty (especially with regards to racism and sexism) and also explores themes of survival and resilience.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}16[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-16)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}17[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-17)^ Butler wrote the novel \"thinking about the future, thinking about the things that we\'re doing now and the kind of future we\'re buying for ourselves, if we\'re not careful.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}18[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-18)^

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Margaret_Atwood_2015.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Margaret_Atwood_2015.jpg/250px-Margaret_Atwood_2015.jpg" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" data-file-height="1091" data-file-width="727" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Margaret_Atwood_2015.jpg/500px-Margaret_Atwood_2015.jpg 2x" width="190" height="285" /></a>
<figcaption><a href="/wiki/Margaret_Atwood" title="Margaret Atwood">Margaret Atwood</a>'s <em><a href="/wiki/Oryx_and_Crake" title="Oryx and Crake">Oryx and Crake</a></em> series is an often cited <a href="/wiki/Utopian_and_dystopian_fiction" title="Utopian and dystopian fiction">dystopian novel</a> in <a href="/wiki/Ecocriticism" title="Ecocriticism">ecocriticism</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

As [scientific knowledge](/wiki/Scientific_consensus_on_climate_change "Scientific consensus on climate change") of the effects of fossil fuel consumption and resulting [increase in atmospheric CO~2~ concentrations](/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions") entered the public and political arena as \"[global warming](/wiki/History_of_climate_change_science "History of climate change science")\",^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}19[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-aiphistory-19)^ human-caused climate change entered works of fiction. [Susan M. Gaines](/wiki/Susan_M._Gaines "Susan M. Gaines")\'s *[Carbon Dreams](/wiki/Carbon_Dreams "Carbon Dreams")* (2000) was an early example of a literary novel that \"tells a story about the devastatingly serious issue of human-induced climate change\", set in the 1980s and published before the term \"cli-fi\" was coined.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}20[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-20)^ [Michael Crichton](/wiki/Michael_Crichton "Michael Crichton")\'s *[State of Fear](/wiki/State_of_Fear "State of Fear")* (2004), a [techno-thriller](/wiki/Techno-thriller "Techno-thriller"), was a bestseller upon its release but was criticised by scientists for portraying climate change as \"a vast pseudo-scientific hoax\" and [rejecting](/wiki/Climate_change_denial "Climate change denial") the scientific consensus on climate change.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}21[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-21)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}22[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-22)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}23[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-23)^ [Sigbjørn Skåden](/wiki/Sigbj%C3%B8rn_Sk%C3%A5den "Sigbjørn Skåden")\'s novel [*Fugl*](/wiki/Fugl_(novel) "Fugl (novel)") (2019) is a [Sámi](/wiki/S%C3%A1mi_people "Sámi people") novel written in Norwegian that weaves together environmental collapse with an allegory of [colonialism](/wiki/Colonialism "Colonialism").

[Margaret Atwood](/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") explored the subject in her dystopian trilogy *[Oryx and Crake](/wiki/Oryx_and_Crake "Oryx and Crake")* (2003), *[The Year of the Flood](/wiki/The_Year_of_the_Flood "The Year of the Flood")* (2009) and *[MaddAddam](/wiki/MaddAddam "MaddAddam")* (2013).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}24[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-24)^ In *Oryx and Crake*, Atwood presents a world where \"social inequality, genetic technology and catastrophic climate change, has finally culminated in some apocalyptic event\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}25[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-PubWeekly-25)^ The novel\'s protagonist, Jimmy, lives in a \"world split between corporate compounds\", [gated communities](/wiki/Gated_communities "Gated communities"){.mw-redirect} that have grown into [city-states](/wiki/City-state "City-state") and pleeblands, which are \"unsafe, populous and polluted\" urban areas where the working classes live.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}25[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-PubWeekly-25)^

In 2016, Indian writer [Amitav Ghosh](/wiki/Amitav_Ghosh "Amitav Ghosh") expressed concern that climate change had \"a much smaller presence in contemporary literary fiction than it does even in public discussion\". In *[The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable](/wiki/The_Great_Derangement:_Climate_Change_and_the_Unthinkable "The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable")*, Ghosh said \"if certain literary forms are unable to negotiate these waters, then they will have failed -- and their failures will have to be counted as an aspect of the broader imaginative and cultural failure that lies at the heart of the climate crisis.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}26[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:4-26)^ In *The Anthropocene Unconscious: Climate Catastrophe Culture*, critic Mark Bould suggests the opposite when he argues that the \"art and literature of our time is pregnant with catastrophe, with weather and water, wildness and weirdness.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}27[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-27)^

By the 2010s, climate fiction had attracted greater prominence and media attention.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}6[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-AsTheWeatherShifts-6)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}28[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-28)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}29[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-29)^ Cultural critic Josephine Livingston at *[The New Republic](/wiki/The_New_Republic "The New Republic")* wrote in 2020 that \"the last decade has seen such a steep rise in sophisticated \'cli-fi\' that some literary publications now devote whole verticals to it. With such various and fertile imaginations at work on the same topic, whether in fiction or nonfiction, the challenge facing the environmental writer now is standing out from the crowd (not to mention the headlines).\" She highlighted [Jeff Vandermeer](/wiki/Jeff_VanderMeer "Jeff VanderMeer")\'s *[Annihilation](/wiki/Annihilation_(VanderMeer_novel) "Annihilation (VanderMeer novel)")* to [Nathaniel Rich](/wiki/Nathaniel_Rich_(novelist) "Nathaniel Rich (novelist)")\'s *Odds Against Tomorrow* as examples.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}30[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-30)^

In [African literature](/wiki/African_literature "African literature"), climate informed novels and short stories have been recently receiving attention as a field of contemporary African literature. Books such as *Eclipse our sins*, by [Tlotlo Tsamaase](/wiki/Tlotlo_Tsamaase "Tlotlo Tsamaase"); *It Doesn't Have to Be This Way*, by [Alistair Mackay](/wiki/Alistair_Mackay_(writer) "Alistair Mackay (writer)") and *Noor*, by [Nnedi Okorafor](/wiki/Nnedi_Okorafor "Nnedi Okorafor"), have been highlighted as notable publications in the genre.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}31[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-africanarguments.org-31)^

## Prominent examples {#Prominent_examples}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Prominent examples")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

The popular science-fiction novelist [Kim Stanley Robinson](/wiki/Kim_Stanley_Robinson "Kim Stanley Robinson") has been writing on the theme for several decades, including his *Science in the Capital* trilogy, which is set in the near future and includes *[Forty Signs of Rain](/wiki/Forty_Signs_of_Rain "Forty Signs of Rain")* (2004), *[Fifty Degrees Below](/wiki/Fifty_Degrees_Below "Fifty Degrees Below")* (2005), and *[Sixty Days and Counting](/wiki/Sixty_Days_and_Counting "Sixty Days and Counting")* (2007). Robert K. J. Killheffer in his review for *[Fantasy & Science Fiction](/wiki/Fantasy_%26_Science_Fiction "Fantasy & Science Fiction"){.mw-redirect}* said \"*Forty Signs of Rain* is a fascinating depiction of the workings of science and politics, and an urgent call to readers to confront the threat of climate change.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}32[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Killheffer-32)^ Robinson\'s climate-themed novel, titled *[New York 2140](/wiki/New_York_2140 "New York 2140")*, was published in March 2017.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}33[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-33)^ It gives a complex portrait of a coastal city that is partly underwater and yet has successfully adapted to climate change in its culture and ecology. Robinson\'s novel *[The Ministry for the Future](/wiki/The_Ministry_for_the_Future "The Ministry for the Future")*, is set in the near future, and follows a subsidiary body, whose mission is to advocate for the world\'s future generations of citizens as if their rights are as valid as the present generation\'s.

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Kim_Stanley_Robinson_(36548718233).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Kim_Stanley_Robinson_%2836548718233%29.jpg/250px-Kim_Stanley_Robinson_%2836548718233%29.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="3840" data-file-width="5760" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Kim_Stanley_Robinson_%2836548718233%29.jpg/500px-Kim_Stanley_Robinson_%2836548718233%29.jpg 2x" width="250" height="167" /></a>
<figcaption>Kim Stanley Robinson's science fiction works frequently include society's response to climate change.</figcaption>
</figure>

British author [J. G. Ballard](/wiki/J._G._Ballard "J. G. Ballard") used the setting of apocalyptic climate change in his early science fiction novels. In *[The Wind from Nowhere](/wiki/The_Wind_from_Nowhere "The Wind from Nowhere")* (1961), civilisation is reduced by persistent hurricane-force winds. *[The Drowned World](/wiki/The_Drowned_World "The Drowned World")* (1962) describes a future of melted ice-caps and rising sea-levels, caused by solar radiation, creating a landscape mirroring the [collective unconscious](/wiki/Collective_unconscious "Collective unconscious") desires of the main characters. In *[The Burning World](/wiki/The_Burning_World_(novel) "The Burning World (novel)")* (1964) a surrealistic psychological landscape is formed by drought due to industrial pollution disrupting the [precipitation](/wiki/Precipitation "Precipitation") cycle.

Similarly, *[The Road](/wiki/The_Road "The Road")* (2006) by [Cormac McCarthy](/wiki/Cormac_McCarthy "Cormac McCarthy") is set after an unspecified apocalypse or environmental catastrophe. It won the [Pulitzer Prize for Fiction](/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Fiction "Pulitzer Prize for Fiction") in 2007. Although it does not explicitly mention climate change, it has been listed by *[The Guardian](/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* as one of the best climate change novels,^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}34[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:0-34)^ and environmentalist [George Monbiot](/wiki/George_Monbiot "George Monbiot") has described it as \"the most important environmental book ever written\" for depicting a world without a [biosphere](/wiki/Biosphere "Biosphere").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}35[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-35)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}36[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-36)^

The novel *[State of Fear](/wiki/State_of_Fear "State of Fear")* by [Michael Crichton](/wiki/Michael_Crichton "Michael Crichton"), published in December 2004, describes a conspiracy by scientists and others to create public panic about global warming.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}37[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-37)^ Crichton had publicly advocated \"skepticism\" of global warming.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}38[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Crichton01-38)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}39[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Crichton02-39)^ His novel describes a group of [eco-terrorists](/wiki/Eco-terrorism "Eco-terrorism") attempting to create [natural disasters](/wiki/Natural_disaster "Natural disaster") to convince the public of the dangers of global warming. It is based upon the idea that there is a deliberately alarmist conspiracy behind [climate change activism](/wiki/Climate_movement "Climate movement"). The book is critical of the [scientific consensus on climate change](/wiki/Scientific_opinion_on_climate_change "Scientific opinion on climate change"){.mw-redirect}. A critique in the BBC News pointed out that \"Crichton\'s trade is to bring pleasurable terror to millions by spinning tales of science gone amok\" and \"To make sure you get his point, Crichton adds a 32-page footnote documenting his own conviction that global warming is an unscientific scare.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}40[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-40)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}41[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Footnotes-41)^

[Ian McEwan](/wiki/Ian_McEwan "Ian McEwan")\'s *[Solar](/wiki/Solar_(novel) "Solar (novel)")* (2010) follows the story of a physicist who discovers a way to fight climate change after managing to derive power from artificial photosynthesis.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}42[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-42)^ [*The Stone Gods*](/wiki/The_Stone_Gods_(novel) "The Stone Gods (novel)") (2007) by [Jeanette Winterson](/wiki/Jeanette_Winterson "Jeanette Winterson") is set on the fictional planet Orbus, a world very like Earth, running out of resources and suffering from the severe effects of climate change. Inhabitants of Orbus hope to take advantage of possibilities offered by a newly discovered planet, Planet Blue, which appears perfect for human life.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}43[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-43)^

Other authors who have used this subject matter include:

-   *[Fallen Angels](/wiki/Fallen_Angels_(science_fiction_novel) "Fallen Angels (science fiction novel)"){.mw-redirect}* (1991) by [Larry Niven](/wiki/Larry_Niven "Larry Niven"), [Jerry Pournelle](/wiki/Jerry_Pournelle "Jerry Pournelle"), and [Michael Flynn](/wiki/Michael_Flynn_(author) "Michael Flynn (author)"){.mw-redirect}. Set in North America in the \"near future\", a radical [technophobic](/wiki/Technophobic "Technophobic"){.mw-redirect} [green](/wiki/Green "Green") movement dramatically cuts greenhouse gas emissions, only to find that manmade global warming was staving off a new [ice age](/wiki/Ice_age "Ice age").
-   *[Mother of Storms](/wiki/Mother_of_Storms "Mother of Storms")* (1994) by [John Barnes](/wiki/John_Barnes_(author) "John Barnes (author)") describes a catastrophic, rapid climate and weather change brought on by a nuclear explosion releasing [clathrate compounds](/wiki/Clathrate_compound "Clathrate compound") from the ocean floor, based on the [clathrate gun hypothesis](/wiki/Clathrate_gun_hypothesis "Clathrate gun hypothesis").
-   *[The Swarm](/wiki/The_Swarm_(Sch%C3%A4tzing_novel) "The Swarm (Schätzing novel)")* (2004) by [Frank Schätzing](/wiki/Frank_Sch%C3%A4tzing "Frank Schätzing"). The book follows an ensemble of protagonists who are investigating what at first appear to be freak events related to the world\'s oceans. Seemingly unrelated events like the destabilization of the continental shelf resulting in a megatsunami, whales attacking a commercial freighter, and an outbreak of an epidemic caused by contaminated lobsters are revealed to be caused by an unknown submarine species trying to defend the oceans against human influence.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}44[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-44)^
-   *Far North* (2009) by [Marcel Theroux](/wiki/Marcel_Theroux "Marcel Theroux"), in which the world is largely uninhabitable due to climate change. However, the novel implies that scientists got it wrong and that it was our actions combating global warming that irrevocably altered the climate.
-   *[Arctic Drift](/wiki/Arctic_Drift "Arctic Drift"){.mw-redirect}* (2008) by [Clive Cussler](/wiki/Clive_Cussler "Clive Cussler") and Dirk Cussler. A [thriller](/wiki/Thriller_(genre) "Thriller (genre)") involving attempts to reverse global warming, a possible war between the [United States](/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Canada](/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and \"a mysterious silvery mineral traced to a long-ago expedition in search of the fabled Northwest Passage.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}45[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-45)^
-   *Devolution of a Species* by M.E. Ellington focuses on the [Gaia hypothesis](/wiki/Gaia_hypothesis "Gaia hypothesis"), and describes the Earth as a single living organism fighting back against humankind.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}46[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-46)\[*[[non-primary\ source\ needed]{title="This claim needs references to reliable secondary sources. (June 2021)"}](/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")*\]^
-   *[The Carbon Diaries: 2015](/wiki/The_Carbon_Diaries:_2015 "The Carbon Diaries: 2015"){.mw-redirect}* (2009) by [Saci Lloyd](/wiki/Saci_Lloyd "Saci Lloyd") is set in a future where power is scarce and the [UK](/wiki/UK "UK"){.mw-redirect} has just begun carbon rationing. The story is told in diary form by Laura Brown, a teenager living in [London](/wiki/London "London") in the aftermath of the Great Storm.
-   [Barbara Kingsolver](/wiki/Barbara_Kingsolver "Barbara Kingsolver")\'s novel, *[Flight Behavior](/wiki/Flight_Behavior "Flight Behavior")* (2012), employs environmental themes and highlights the potential [effects of global warming](/wiki/Effects_of_global_warming "Effects of global warming"){.mw-redirect} on the [monarch butterfly](/wiki/Monarch_butterfly "Monarch butterfly").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}47[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-47)^
-   Norwegian author [Maja Lunde](/wiki/Maja_Lunde "Maja Lunde") has released a \"Climate Quartet\" of novels, beginning with *Bienes histore* (*The History of Bees*) in 2015, which examines [pollinator decline](/wiki/Pollinator_decline "Pollinator decline") through a number of human storylines throughout history, followed by *The End of the Ocean* (2017), *Przewalski\'s Horse* (2019) and an upcoming fourth instalment.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}48[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-48)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}49[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-49)^
-   [Rajat Chaudhuri](/wiki/Rajat_Chaudhuri "Rajat Chaudhuri")'s novel, *The Butterfly Effect* (2018), is a dystopian cli-fi with thriller undercurrents that deals with [genetic engineering](/wiki/Genetic_engineering "Genetic engineering"), scientific experiments gone wrong and the effect of intertwined disasters.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}50[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-50)^ This book has been listed by Book Riot as one of \"50 Must-Read Eco Disasters In Fiction\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}51[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-51)^
-   *The New Wilderness* (2020) by [Diane Cook](/wiki/Diane_Cook "Diane Cook") is set in North America where climate change has affected the natural environment. It was shortlisted for the [2020 Booker Prize](/wiki/2020_Booker_Prize "2020 Booker Prize").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}52[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-52)^
-   *[Bewilderment](/wiki/Bewilderment "Bewilderment")* (2021) by [Richard Powers](/wiki/Richard_Powers "Richard Powers") was shortlisted for the [2021 Booker Prize](/wiki/2021_Booker_Prize "2021 Booker Prize"). It was also longlisted for the 2021 [National Book Award for Fiction](/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Fiction "National Book Award for Fiction").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}53[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-53)^ It was selected by [Oprah Winfrey](/wiki/Oprah_Winfrey "Oprah Winfrey") as part of *[Oprah\'s Book Club](/wiki/Oprah%27s_Book_Club_(TV_series) "Oprah's Book Club (TV series)")* on 28 September 2021.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}54[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-54)^

\

### Description of apocalyptic scenarios {#Description_of_apocalyptic_scenarios}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Description of apocalyptic scenarios")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

\"[Climate apocalypse scenarios](/wiki/Climate_change_and_civilizational_collapse "Climate change and civilizational collapse")\" are explored in multiple [science fiction](/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") works. For example, in *[The Wind from Nowhere](/wiki/The_Wind_from_Nowhere "The Wind from Nowhere")* (1961), civilization is devastated by persistent hurricane-force winds, and *[The Drowned World](/wiki/The_Drowned_World "The Drowned World")* (1962) describes a future of melted ice-caps and [rising sea-levels](/wiki/Rising_sea_levels "Rising sea levels"){.mw-redirect} caused by [solar radiation](/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}55[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-55)^ In *[The Burning World](/wiki/The_Burning_World_(novel) "The Burning World (novel)")* (1964, later retitled *The Drought*) his climate catastrophe is human-made, a [drought](/wiki/Drought "Drought") due to disruption of the precipitation cycle by [industrial pollution](/wiki/Pollution "Pollution").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}56[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-56)^

[Octavia E. Butler](/wiki/Octavia_E._Butler "Octavia E. Butler")\'s *[Parable of the Sower](/wiki/Parable_of_the_Sower_(novel) "Parable of the Sower (novel)")* (1993) imagines a near-future for the United States where climate change, wealth inequality, and corporate greed cause apocalyptic chaos. Here, and in sequel [*Parable of the Talents*](/wiki/Parable_of_the_Talents_(novel) "Parable of the Talents (novel)") (1998), Butler dissects how instability and political demagoguery exacerbate society\'s underlying cruelty (especially with regards to racism and sexism) and also explores themes of survival and resilience.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}57[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-57)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}58[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-58)^ Butler wrote the novel \"thinking about the future, thinking about the things that we\'re doing now and the kind of future we\'re buying for ourselves, if we\'re not careful.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}59[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-59)^

[Margaret Atwood](/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") explored the subject in her dystopian trilogy *[Oryx and Crake](/wiki/Oryx_and_Crake "Oryx and Crake")* (2003), *[The Year of the Flood](/wiki/The_Year_of_the_Flood "The Year of the Flood")* (2009) and *[MaddAddam](/wiki/MaddAddam "MaddAddam")* (2013).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}60[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-60)^ In *Oryx and Crake*, Atwood presents a world where \"social inequality, genetic technology and catastrophic climate change, has finally culminated in some apocalyptic event\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}61[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-PubWeekly2-61)^

## Anthologies and collections {#Anthologies_and_collections}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Anthologies and collections")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

-   *Welcome to the Greenhouse* (2011) US edited by [Gordon Van Gelder](/wiki/Gordon_Van_Gelder "Gordon Van Gelder")
-   *Loosed Upon the World: The Saga Anthology of Climate Fiction* (2015) US edited by [John Joseph Adams](/wiki/John_Joseph_Adams "John Joseph Adams")
-   *Drowned Worlds* (2016) UK edited by [Jonathan Strahan](/wiki/Jonathan_Strahan "Jonathan Strahan")
-   *Possible Solutions* (2017) US by [Helen Phillips](/wiki/Helen_Phillips_(novelist) "Helen Phillips (novelist)") -- Many of the short stories concern climate change.
-   Author and editor Bruce Meyer and creative writing professor at Georgian College edited a 2017 anthology of stories about \"changing ocean conditions, the widening disappearance of species, genetically modified organisms, increasing food shortages, mass migrations of refugees, and the hubris behind our provoking Mother Earth herself\", which he labels as \"cli-fi\". The anthology includes works by George McWhirter, Richard Van Camp, Holly Schofield, Linda Rogers, Sean Virgo, Rati Mehrotra, Geoffrey W. Cole, Phil Dwyer, Kate Story, Leslie Goodreid, Nina Munteanu, Halli Villegas, John Oughton, Frank Westcott, Wendy Bone, Peter Timmerman, and Lynn Hutchinson-Lee.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}70[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-70)^
-   *Meteotopia - Futures of Climate (In)Justice* (2022) Collection of short stories on climate and environment by authors of the [Global South](/wiki/Global_South "Global South"){.mw-redirect}.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}31[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-africanarguments.org-31)^
-   *The Routledge Anthology of Climate Fiction, Volume One* (2024) edited by [Bill Gillard](/w/index.php?title=Bill_Gillard&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bill Gillard (page does not exist)"){.new}, a short story collection that makes the argument that the literature of climate change started much earlier than the critical consensus would have it, as early as the 1870s when the effects of industrialization were being explored by science-fiction writers and other artists.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}71[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-71)^

## Influence {#Influence}

[[\[]{.mw-editsection-bracket}[edit](/w/index.php?title=Climate_fiction&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Influence")[\]]{.mw-editsection-bracket}]{.mw-editsection}

Many journalists, literary critics, and scholars have speculated about the potential influence of climate fiction on the beliefs of its readers. To date, three empirical studies have examined this question.

A controlled experiment found that reading climate fiction short stories \"had small but significant positive effects on several important beliefs and attitudes about global warming -- observed immediately after participants read the stories\", though \"these effects diminished to statistical nonsignificance after a one-month interval\". However, the authors note that \"the effects of a single exposure in an artificial setting may represent a lower bound of the real-world effects. Reading climate fiction in the real world often involves multiple exposures and longer narratives\", such as novels, \"which may result in larger and longer-lasting impacts\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}72[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-72)^

A survey of readers found that readers of climate fiction \"are younger, more liberal, and more concerned about climate change than nonreaders\", and that climate fiction \"reminds concerned readers of the severity of climate change while impelling them to imagine environmental futures and consider the impact of climate change on human and nonhuman life. However, the actions that resulted from readers\' heightened consciousness reveal that awareness is only as valuable as the cultural messages about possible actions to take that are in circulation. Moreover, the responses of some readers suggest that works of climate fiction might lead some people to associate climate change with intensely negative emotions, which could prove counterproductive to efforts at environmental engagement or persuasion.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}73[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-73)^

Finally, an empirical study focused on the popular novel *[The Water Knife](/wiki/The_Water_Knife "The Water Knife")* found that cautionary climate fiction set in a dystopic future can be effective at educating readers about climate injustice and leading readers to empathize with the victims of climate change, including [environmental migrants](/wiki/Environmental_migrant "Environmental migrant"). However, its results suggest that dystopic climate narratives might lead to support for [reactionary responses to climate change](/wiki/Ecofascism "Ecofascism"). Based on this result, it cautioned that \"not all climate fiction is progressive\", despite the hopes of many authors, critics, and readers.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}74[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-74)^
